summary: DMARC lets domains state policies for email validation, disposition and reporting, but it can cause interoperability problems when messages do not flow directly from the author's domain to the receiver, such as through mailing lists. This informational document describes these issues and discusses possible mitigations.

eli5.summary: Some rules say to throw away mail that fails a sender check. But mail passed along by a group list can look fake to the rules. This describes why that happens and what can be done.

how to fix dmarc with mailing lists
subtitle: Why strict DMARC policies break mailing lists, forwarders and other mail that does not travel straight from author to reader.

tldr.problem: DMARC lets a domain ask receivers to quarantine or reject mail that fails authentication, but mail that is forwarded, relayed or modified on the way can fail those checks even though everyone involved considers it legitimate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogues the causes (identifier alignment, forwarding, message modification), maps them onto the components of the Internet Mail Architecture, and lists mitigations for senders, receivers and resenders.
tldr.outcome: It is an analysis, not a standard. It offers workarounds, several of which it admits have side effects, and notes that some proposed fixes were still Internet-Drafts.

today: RFC 7960 is an Informational document and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the DMARC situation as of September 2016, and some mitigations it mentions were still drafts at that time.

sections.title: Indirect Email Flows Meet DMARC
sections.content:
DMARC (RFC 7489) lets a domain publish policies for how mail claiming to come from it should be validated, handled and reported. With restrictive policies it runs into trouble whenever mail is sourced by a third party, transformed or rerouted. The RFC calls any path where mail does not go straight from the author's administrative domain to the recipient an indirect email flow.

The RFC singles out mailing lists as the most visible casualty. It also says that domains asserting p=none, and messages that pass standard DMARC validation, have no interoperability issues. Mail that breaks IETF email specifications but is wanted by recipients is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A rule meant to stop fake letters also catches real letters that were passed along by someone else, like a letter handed from friend to friend.

sections.title: Why Mail Fails DMARC
sections.content:
DMARC relies on DKIM (RFC 6376) and SPF (RFC 7208) to produce Authenticated Identifiers. To count, an identifier's domain must align with the domain in the RFC5322.From header field. In strict mode the match must be exact. In relaxed mode the two need only share the same Organizational Domain. Some mitigations in the RFC work only with relaxed mode.

Three causes are described. First, alignment itself: DKIM signatures must come from the same Organizational Domain as the From domain, and some implementations mishandle messages with multiple DKIM signatures. SPF identifiers come from the RFC5321.MailFrom domain, falling back to the HELO/EHLO domain when MailFrom is empty, as in notification messages.

Second, forwarding: if a forwarder keeps the original MailFrom, SPF fails unless the forwarder is authorized by the originator. If it replaces MailFrom with its own domain, SPF may pass but will not align with the From header. Either way DKIM must carry the result.

Third, message modification: changing content breaks most DKIM signatures. The DKIM length flag is seldom used because of its security issues, and a few verifiers have trouble with relaxed canonicalization.
sections.eli5: The check compares the name on the envelope with the name on the letter. Passing a letter along changes the envelope, and editing the letter breaks its seal, so the check can fail.

sections.title: Where Things Break in the Mail Architecture
sections.content:
Using the components of the Internet Mail Architecture (RFC 5598), the RFC shows where trouble appears. A submission agent can face problems when the From domain lies outside its own administrative domain: the RFC lists partially open relays, embedded devices, devices sending on behalf of a user, email service providers and calendaring software. Transfer agents may re-encode messages, rewrite headers or alter content, all of which break DKIM. Sieve filters at delivery can add or delete headers.

Mediators are hardest hit because they exist to re-post and often modify mail. The RFC covers Aliases, ReSenders, Mailing Lists, Gateways and Boundary Filters. Mailing lists commonly prepend subject tags, add footers, strip MIME parts and so on, each of which invalidates a DKIM signature.

A list can also hurt itself: it may read DMARC-related bounces as undeliverable mail and suspend or remove subscribers whose receivers enforce DMARC.

Flows can also be combined, for example a list subscription delivered to a university address that forwards to a freemail account.
sections.eli5: Every helper that touches a letter on its way, such as a list, a forwarder or a scanner, might change it or its envelope, and each change can make the sender check fail.

sections.title: Mitigations in Use
sections.content:
The RFC warns that these may not be best practices and may violate conventions. For senders, it suggests aligning MailFrom or HELO/EHLO with the From domain, DKIM-signing notification messages with an aligned domain, using a From address under the sender's control with the original in Reply-To, and keeping DKIM signatures robust by signing fewer headers and using relaxed canonicalization. Using the DKIM length tag is discouraged.

For receivers: update DKIM libraries to process all valid signatures, and use local policy overrides, for example based on lists of known forwarders.

For resenders, the main idea is to use a From header they control and sign with an aligned domain. For mailing lists the options are rewriting the From to the list's domain (with the author in the display name), wrapping the message in a message/rfc822 part, not modifying the message, or rejecting posts from domains with a DMARC policy other than p=none. Each has costs, such as hard-to-read messages in some clients or unhappy members. Lists should also avoid acting on DMARC-related bounces, using enhanced status codes (RFC 3463, RFC 7372).
sections.eli5: People can fix this by putting their own return address on re-sent letters, by not editing letters, or by teaching receivers which helpers to trust. Every fix has a small price.

sections.title: Proposed Mitigations and Security Notes
sections.content:
Some mitigations were based on Internet-Drafts still in progress and are described only as an exploratory path that should not be used in production. They include third-party authorization schemes, ways to isolate mailing list alterations, recording reversible transformations at each hop, conditional DKIM signatures, and extending Authentication-Results (RFC 7601) across multiple hops. The RFC also muses about a new communication path with the user to authorize mailing lists as proxies for authentication.

The Security Considerations section notes that DMARC rejections on indirect flows can cause accidental denial of service, that third-party DKIM key management needs care, and that rewriting the From address to an artificial domain should not be done with just any domain.
sections.eli5: People were still inventing better fixes, like a way for you to say which lists you trust. The RFC warns that sneaky senders could misuse some of the quick fixes.
